claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA nanoscale multilayers is governed by an interplay between interfacial dislocation activity and SRO-mediated diffusion.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion enhance SRO-mediated diffusion mechanisms.
Sustained uniaxial loading at elevated temperature will induce creep deformation.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
SRO regions facilitate localized atomic rearrangements.
Localized atomic rearrangements in SRO regions contribute to creep through diffusion-assisted deformation.
The balance between interfacial dislocation resistance and SRO-mediated diffusion determines overall deformation behavior.
The initial creep rate will be low because of interface strengthening.
The creep rate will increase over time as SRO-mediated diffusion becomes dominant.
The transition from interface-dominated to diffusion-dominated creep depends on temperature and stress.
The starting creep behavior is dominated by dislocation activity at FCC/BCC interfaces, with minimal diffusion contribution.
The proposed behavior applies only to nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers under diffusion-active conditions that avoid melting and immediate fracture.
